h: Making the most of a crowded, curious hall
p: The museum began when General Augustus Pitt-Rivers gave his collection to the University of Oxford in 1884. He was fascinated by how objects change and develop over time, which is why so much of the museum is laid out by type rather than by place. Since then the collection has grown massively, and it holds hundreds of thousands of objects.

Like many museums with collections gathered in the days of empire, the Pitt Rivers has been looking hard at how it tells its stories. In 2020 it removed a number of human remains from display, including its well-known shrunken heads, after an ethical review. You'll see new labels and displays that reflect this work as you go round, and they make for thoughtful reading.

How long to allow? Even an hour feels packed, but two hours lets you hunt out the cases that grab you. Bring your patience and your curiosity rather than a plan. Kids often love it as a giant treasure hunt, so pick a theme together, like masks or boats, and see how many you can spot.

Make a proper Oxford day of it. On the way through, the Natural History Museum is famous for its dodo and its dinosaur skeletons. Just a short walk away are the University Parks for a riverside stroll, while the Ashmolean Museum, the Radcliffe Camera and the Bodleian Library are all within easy reach in the city centre. Grab lunch in the Covered Market or a pint in one of the old pubs to round things off.
